title: Built to Last: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies
author: Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras
target_audience: Anyone interested in long-term organizational success
core_themes: What distinguishes truly exceptional and enduring companies
The importance of core ideology (values and purpose)
Balancing preservation of core values with willingness to change and adapt
Myth-busting: visionary companies are not dependent on charismatic leaders
Incremental progress (clock building vs. time telling)
Cultivating a culture of innovation, experimentation, and consistent improvement
primary_purpose: To identify and analyze the core practices and principles that enable certain companies to sustain exceptional performance and thrive over decades, providing actionable insights for building organizations that endure.

structure_format.narrative_style: Research-driven, analytical, case study based, accessible and engaging
structure_format.organization: Structured around key habits and characteristics, with each chapter focused on a major theme supported by case studies and empirical research
features: In-depth comparison between visionary companies and less successful industry peers
Key concept summaries at chapter ends
Clear frameworks (e.g., clock building vs. time telling, preserve the core/stimulate progress)
Real-world examples and in-depth company case studies

key_concepts_lessons: Visionary companies emphasize core values and purpose beyond just profit.
Building organizational capabilities (clock building) is more lasting than charisma or single ideas (time telling).
Visionary companies cultivate cultures that stimulate progress and innovation while preserving their core ideology.
"Try a lot of stuff and keep what works"—experimentation is essential.
Visionary companies set Big Hairy Audacious Goals (BHAGs) to inspire progress.
Success rests on consistency over time rather than dramatic, short-term change or one-time breakthrough.
notable_features: Based on six years of research at Stanford Graduate School of Business
Direct comparative analysis of 18 pairs of companies (visionary vs. comparison companies)
Synthesizes theory with actionable frameworks and models
Popularized concepts like ‘core ideology’ and ‘clock building’
Led to a sequel, ‘Good to Great’
cultural_historical_context: Published in the mid-1990s, 'Built to Last' responded to questions about why some companies outlast others amid rapid technological and economic changes. It set the stage for a renewed focus on corporate vision and values during a period of management fads and short-term thinking.
reception_impact: International bestseller with significant influence on business thinking and management practice
Widely adopted in MBA programs and leadership training
Frequently cited and referenced by business leaders
Criticism in later years over whether all ‘visionary’ companies maintained stellar performance, but central frameworks remain influential
comparable_titles: Good to Great by Jim Collins
In Search of Excellence by Tom Peters and Robert H. Waterman Jr.
The Innovator's Dilemma by Clayton M. Christensen
First, Break All the Rules by Marcus Buckingham and Curt Coffman
